title: Hubble's festive view of a grand star-forming region
caption: The star cluster R136 in the 30 Doradus Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: 30 Doradus · constellation Dorado · about 170000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and F. Paresce (INAF-IASF, Bologna, Italy), R. O'Connell (University of Virginia, Charlottesville), and the Wide Field Camera 3 Science Oversight Committee

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: Hundreds of brilliant blue stars sit among warm, glowing clouds in this Hubble view, the most detailed yet of the largest stellar nursery in our galactic neighborhood. The young cluster at its heart, R136, has existed for only a few million years and lies in the 30 Doradus Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.
Many of these blue stars are among the most massive known, several over 100 times the mass of the Sun. They will probably explode as supernovae within a few million years.

Their ultraviolet light and fierce stellar winds are carving deep cavities in the hydrogen cloud where they were born. The result is a landscape of pillars, ridges and valleys, with a dark central area shaped roughly like a holiday tree. When the winds slam into dense walls of gas they produce shocks, which may be setting off a new wave of star birth.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.60 x 2.66 arcminutes) and distance (170000 light years), the frame spans roughly 129 × 132 light-years. Its light set out about 170,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in ultraviolet, visible and red light. Blue shows light from the hottest, most massive stars, green the glow of oxygen, and red fluorescing hydrogen.
understand.eye: Part of this light is ultraviolet, invisible to the eye, and the colors were chosen to separate different gases rather than to show what the eye would see.

explore: The Large Magellanic Cloud's motion around the Milky Way may have triggered the cluster's birth, by compressing its gas through gravity or by pressure as it plowed through our galaxy's halo. R136 is a rare nearby example of the super star clusters common in the early Universe. The image spans about 100 light-years.
alt: A cluster of bright blue stars amid glowing clouds carved into pillars, ridges and valleys, with a dark tree-shaped region near the center.
